lead: At one instant, a rigid body in plane motion can be treated as if it were rotating about a single point, the instantaneous centre I. That point has zero velocity at that instant. Draw a line perpendicular to the velocity at any point; I lies somewhere on that line. Two points give two lines, and their intersection is I. Then v = ωr gives every point's speed about I. This is a quick velocity tool for linkages, rolling wheels and sliding bars.
prereq: You need: 6.2 for plane motion as translation plus rotation, 6.3 for vB = vA + ω × rBA, and basic geometry of perpendiculars.

sections.h3: The point with zero velocity at this instant

blocks.text: At a chosen instant, every point P of a rigid body in plane motion has some velocity v<sub>P</sub>. Draw the line through P perpendicular to v<sub>P</sub>. If the body is rotating about some point I at that instant, then v<sub>P</sub> must be perpendicular to the line IP. So I lies on that perpendicular line. Two points P and Q give two perpendiculars; where they meet is the instantaneous centre I. The point I can lie on the body, outside it, or far away; it is a geometric construction, not a physical pin.

Use I exactly as a fixed centre for this one instant. The speed of P about I is v<sub>P</sub> = ω r<sub>P</sub>, where v<sub>P</sub> is the speed of P in m/s, ω is the angular speed of the body in rad/s, and r<sub>P</sub> is the distance IP in m. The velocity direction is perpendicular to IP, with the sense given by the rotation. At I, r = 0, so v = 0.

blocks.where: v<sub>P</sub> is speed of point P in m/s; ω is angular speed in rad/s; r<sub>P</sub> is distance from I to P in m.

blocks.text: When two velocities are parallel and unequal, their perpendiculars coincide, so I lies on the line joining the points; place it so the distances from I are in the ratio of the speeds. When the velocities are equal and parallel, the body has pure translation and I is at infinity. Some syllabi call this the instantaneous center of rotation, or ICR.

sections.h3: Rolling wheel and bar sliding on floor and wall

blocks.text: A wheel of radius R rolling without slipping is the standard example. At the instant shown, the contact point C with the ground has zero velocity, so C is the instantaneous centre. The centre O is distance R from C, so v<sub>O</sub> = ωR. The top point T is distance 2R from C, so v<sub>T</sub> = 2ωR, in the same direction as O but twice the speed. This is why the top of a rolling wheel moves faster than the hub.

A bar with one end on a floor and the other on a wall is another common case. End A slides along the floor, so its velocity is horizontal; the perpendicular at A is vertical. End B slides along the wall, so its velocity is vertical; the perpendicular at B is horizontal. Their intersection I is the instantaneous centre. Distances IA and IB follow from the geometry at that instant. Then v<sub>A</sub> = ω IA and v<sub>B</sub> = ω IB. As the bar slides, I moves, so the construction must be repeated at each instant.
The worked example below is the floor-wall bar: at this instant end A is on the floor and end B is on the wall. The same two perpendiculars locate I, and the same formula gives ω.

The instantaneous centre is a velocity shortcut. In general plane motion the instantaneous centre is not a fixed axis: the material point at I has zero velocity, but generally nonzero acceleration, and I generally moves to a new position at the next instant. Do not use fixed-axis acceleration formulas such as aP = ω² rP or aP = α rP about a moving I. Use 6.3 for acceleration. Exception: if the body rotates about a fixed axis, I is fixed on that axis, the acceleration at I is zero, and fixed-axis formulas apply about that axis.

If I is at infinity, the body has pure translation: ω = 0 and every point has the same velocity. The formula v = ωr then needs a limit, not a finite radius. If the body rotates about a fixed axis, I is on that axis. For general plane motion, I changes with time and is not generally the mass centre. The relative-motion method and the instantaneous-centre method give the same velocity; choose the one with less geometry. Kinetics needs forces and the mass centre, so move to 6.5 after velocity.

figure.caption: Perpendiculars to v_A and v_B meet at I. The distances IA = 1.2 m and IB = 0.9 m are the radii used in v = ωr.

spec.aria: A bar with end A moving right and end B moving down; perpendiculars meet at instantaneous centre I, with distances 1.2 m and 0.9 m.

examples.question: At one instant, end A of a 1.5 m bar is at (0.9, 0) m and moves right at 2.0 m/s. End B is at (0, 1.2) m and moves down at 1.5 m/s. Locate the instantaneous centre I and find the angular velocity of the bar.
steps: Velocity at A is horizontal to the right. Its perpendicular is the vertical line x = 0.9 m.
Velocity at B is vertical downward. Its perpendicular is the horizontal line y = 1.2 m.
Distances: IA = 1.2 m and IB = 0.9 m.
At A: v_A = ω IA, so ω = 2.0 ÷ 1.2 = 1.6667 rad/s. At B: ω = 1.5 ÷ 0.9 = 1.6667 rad/s, which agrees.
Direction: A moves right about I, so the rotation is counterclockwise; B moves down about I in the same sense.
examples.answer: I = (0.9, 1.2) m and the angular velocity is 1.6667 rad/s counterclockwise.
examples.check: import math; Ax, Ay = 0.9, 0.0; Bx, By = 0.0, 1.2; vA = 2.0; vB = 1.5; Ix = Ax; Iy = By; IA = math.hypot(Ax-Ix, Ay-Iy); IB = math.hypot(Bx-Ix, By-Iy); omega_A = vA/IA; omega_B = vB/IB; print(Ix); print(Iy); print(round((omega_A+omega_B)/2, 4))

traps: In general plane motion, using I to calculate acceleration with a = ω²r or a = αr as if I were a fixed centre. The material point at I has zero velocity, but not generally zero acceleration, and I moves. Exception: fixed-axis rotation, where I is fixed and fixed-axis formulas apply about that axis.
Treating a moving I as fixed in general plane motion. I generally moves, so at the next instant it is a different point. Exception: fixed-axis rotation, where I is a fixed point on the axis.
Forgetting direction: v is perpendicular to the line from I to the point; a sign slip reverses the sense of rotation.
In rolling without slipping, taking the wheel centre as I. The contact point with the ground is I at that instant.
For pure translation, trying to use a finite I. I is at infinity and ω = 0.

quiz.q: What is the velocity of the instantaneous centre at the instant used to locate it?
quiz.a: Zero. That is the defining property.

quiz.q: Why does a perpendicular to a point's velocity contain the instantaneous centre?
quiz.a: For rotation about I, the velocity of the point is perpendicular to the line joining it to I. So the line from the point to I is perpendicular to the velocity.

quiz.q: A wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping at 4.2 m/s. Find the instantaneous centre and the angular speed.
quiz.a: The contact point with the ground is I. ω = v ÷ R = 4.2 ÷ 0.35 = 12 rad/s.

quiz.q: A body has a finite instantaneous centre I. Is the acceleration of the material point at I also zero? Explain.
quiz.a: Not necessarily. I has zero velocity at that instant, but I moves and the body can have angular acceleration. Use relative-motion acceleration, not fixed-axis formulas about I.

quiz.q: At one instant, point P has v = 3 m/s and the distance from the instantaneous centre to P is 0.6 m. Find ω.
For a body in pure translation, where is the instantaneous centre and what happens to v = ωr?
quiz.a: I is at infinity and ω = 0. The product ωr is finite in the limit and equals the common velocity; a finite I cannot be used.

beyond: Not for the exam. In robotics, the instantaneous centre is used to check the motion of planar linkages and wheeled mobile robots; each link has its own instantaneous centre. In vehicle dynamics, the same idea underlies the roll centre and the instant centre of a suspension linkage. Search next for 'instant centre of rotation linkage' and 'Ackermann steering instantaneous centre'.
